opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
When I read Romans and the words of Jesus about the sparrows together, I see a God who is trying to show us both the reality of our condition and the depth of His love. Paul tells us that through one man, Adam, sin entered the world and death through sin. We do not need much convincing of this. We see brokenness everywhere. We see it in our relationships, our bodies, our fears, our losses, and our disappointments. We know something is wrong because even before there was a written law, death still reigned. Humanity was already carrying a wound that it could not heal itself. Yet Paul does not stop with Adam because the purpose of Romans is not to convince us that sin is powerful. We already know that. The purpose is to show us that Christ is greater. Adam brought a wound to humanity, but Christ brought the cure. Adam's act affected all who came after him, but Christ's gift is not like the transgression. The damage caused by sin is real, but the grace of God is greater still. Where sin spreads, grace reaches further. Where death claims victory, Christ opens the door to life. The message is not that we are trapped by what Adam did. The message is that we are invited into what Christ has done.

Then Jesus speaks of the sparrows. Not one sparrow falls to the ground apart from the Father's knowledge. Jesus does not say the sparrow never falls. He does not say suffering never comes. He does not say faithful people will avoid pain. What He says is that nothing happens outside the loving gaze of the Father. If God sees a sparrow that most people would never notice, then He certainly sees the person who is carrying grief, fear, loneliness, sickness, uncertainty, or regret. The Father is not distant from our suffering. He is aware of it. He knows every burden before we speak it, every fear before we confess it, every tear before it falls.

Together, these readings reveal something profound. Romans answers the question, "What has God done about the human condition?" Matthew answers the question, "Does God see what I am going through?" Romans says Christ has entered our brokenness and overcome what we could never overcome ourselves. Matthew says that while we walk through this life, we are never unseen, forgotten, or abandoned. The same God who provides salvation for the world notices the sparrow, counts the hairs on our heads, and knows the details of our lives.
